summary: Defines a SIP media feature tag and option tag for indicating support for ICE. The feature tag lets a user agent tell its registrar it supports ICE, and the option tag lets a call require it. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Before a call starts, a phone can wave a flag saying it knows how to find a path through firewalls. This defines the flag.

questions: how does sip indicate ice support
what is the ice option tag

how to require ice in sip
why does sip need an ice option tag
subtitle: Two small SIP labels that say whether a phone can do ICE, and let a caller insist on it.

tldr.problem: ICE only works if both ends support it, and a SIP domain usually has some phones that do and some that do not. Proxies need a way to tell, and callers sometimes want to refuse a call that cannot use ICE.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a media feature tag, sip.ice, that a user agent puts in the Contact header field of REGISTER requests, and an option tag, ice, that goes in the Require header field of an INVITE.
tldr.outcome: A registrar can track which devices support ICE so a proxy can route a call through a gateway when needed, and a caller can make a call fail rather than proceed without ICE.

today: RFC 5768 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on ICE as defined in RFC 5245.

sections.title: Why ICE Needs a Signal
sections.content:
SIP sessions are set up with the offer/answer exchange of Session Description Protocol (SDP) messages defined in RFC 3264. These messages carry IP addresses, which is a known problem through Network Address Translators (NATs). Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE), defined in RFC 5245, extends SDP so that agents gather several candidate addresses, put them all in the offer or answer, and use peer-to-peer STUN connectivity checks (RFC 5389) to find one that works.

This RFC adds two labels for SIP user agents that use ICE: a media feature tag named sip.ice and a SIP option tag named ice.
sections.eli5: Some phones know a clever trick for getting calls through home routers. This RFC gives them a way to say so.

sections.title: Gateways and Mandatory ICE
sections.content:
ICE needs both endpoints to support it. Inside one domain, some user agents will support ICE and some will not. To ease deployment, the RFC expects domains to use gateways that act as ICE agents on one side and as non-ICE agents on the other. A call from domain A into domain B could then use ICE even if the device in domain B does not. When domain B receives a call, though, it must know whether to send it through such a gateway or straight to the device. The sip.ice tag lets the registrar track that, and a proxy can use it to decide.

The second motivation is requiring ICE. ICE falls back to non-ICE operation when the answerer lacks it, but an offerer may prefer to abort the call. Typically that is because it would choose a different m/c-line address for a non-ICE peer than for an ICE-capable one. For this, the ice option tag can be placed in the Require header field of an INVITE.
sections.eli5: A building might have a helper at the door who translates for visitors who do not speak the new language. The door needs to know which rooms need the helper. Also, a caller may say, "only connect me if you speak the new language."

sections.title: The sip.ice Media Feature Tag
sections.content:
The sip.ice media feature tag, from the framework in RFC 3840, indicates support for ICE. An agent supports ICE if it is either a lite or full implementation and so can include candidate attributes in an SDP offer or answer for at least one transport protocol.

An agent that supports ICE SHOULD include the tag in the Contact header field of its REGISTER requests and OPTION responses. It MAY include it in an INVITE or INVITE response, but that is redundant with the ICE attributes in the SDP.

The tag cannot always be trusted to describe the other side. When an INVITE has no offer, the callee will be the offerer and cannot use the presence or absence of the tag to learn whether the caller supports ICE. With third-party call control (RFC 3725), the caller may be a controller that does or does not support ICE, while the answerer may be an agent that does or does not.
sections.eli5: The flag goes on the phone's name tag when it signs in. It also works as a hint, but not a promise, about the other side of a call.

sections.title: The ice Option Tag
sections.content:
The ice option tag is meant to be used only with the Require header field. When it is in the Require header field of an INVITE, the User Agent Server (UAS) must support ICE in order to process the call.

It SHOULD NOT be used with the Supported header field (this includes responses to OPTION requests). The media feature tag is the one and only mechanism for indicating support for ICE. The definition of support is the same as for the media feature tag: a full or lite implementation able to include candidate attributes for at least one transport protocol.
sections.eli5: The option tag is a rule on the invitation: "you must know the trick to come to this party." It is never used to just say "I know the trick," because the other flag does that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious intermediary might insert a Require header field with the ice option tag. If the UAS does not support ICE, a call that would have worked fails. The RFC notes this is not specific to ICE and can be done with any option tag. The attack is prevented by using the SIPS mechanism from RFC 3261.

An intermediary might also remove the media feature tag from a REGISTER or OPTIONS request, which could make a call skip ICE processing it would otherwise use. The SIPS mechanism prevents this attack too.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky in the middle could scribble on the invitation or erase the flag. Sending the message over a protected path stops that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the SIP option tag ice, described as identifying the ICE extension and, when present in a Require header field, indicating that ICE is required by an agent.

It also registers the media feature tag sip.ice in the SIP tree defined in RFC 3840. Its ASN.1 identifier is 1.3.6.1.8.4.22 and its value is Boolean. The typical use given is routing a call to a phone that can support ICE.
sections.eli5: Both names are written into the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

items.title: sip.ice (media feature tag)
items.text: Goes in the Contact header field of REGISTER requests and OPTION responses to say the agent supports ICE.

items.title: ice (option tag)
items.text: Goes in the Require header field of an INVITE to say the UAS must support ICE for the call to proceed.
